arXiv:2611.14033v1 [cs.CV] 10 Nov 2026

Few-Step Streaming Video
Generation via Condition Shifting

Deyuan Liu1,2,3,∗  Jungang Li1,2,∗  Kaiwen Zheng1,2,∗  Kai Jiang1,2,∗  Jintao Chen1,2
Yaole Wang1,2  Ming Lin1,2  Tao Lin3,‡  Jianfei Chen1,2,‡  Jun Zhu1,2,‡  Jintao Zhang1,2,‡ Affiliation: 1Tsinghua University  2Shengshu Technology  3Westlake University
Abstract

Few-step sampling reduces the cost of streaming video generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network, which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator. We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator. The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters. This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar’s frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner, with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison. Compared with S2-Avatar, APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606). Human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0%+30.0\% net preference, followed by consistency and video quality at +4.3%+4.3\% each. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability is unchanged. Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4%4.4\% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2%9.2\% shorter mean iteration time than DMD.

††footnotetext: *Co-first authorship. ‡Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow models produce high-quality videos through repeated network evaluations (Brooks et al., 2024, Google DeepMind, 2025, Wan et al., 2025, Seedance et al., 2026). Streaming generation incurs this cost for every new block, making few-step sampling particularly valuable for long sequences. Distillation reduces the number of evaluations (Song et al., 2023, Salimans and Ho, 2022, Zheng et al., 2025b), while the resulting generator must preserve visual quality, maintain characters and scenes, and respond to changing instructions. shows APEX video examples of object interaction and storytelling.

Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises generated samples through the difference between reference and generated-distribution scores (Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a). A frozen pretrained teacher supplies the reference estimate, while a separate fake-score network learns from current generator outputs. For large video backbones, maintaining this auxiliary network adds training memory and computation. Its estimate must also track the generator as the output distribution changes, requiring coordination of their optimization settings and updates. This motivates learning the fake estimate within the generator.

TwinFlow (Cheng et al., 2026) and the original APEX (Liu et al., 2026c) show how generation and distribution estimation can share a network. We extend APEX’s condition shifting to streaming video: the original text condition selects generation, and its shifted version selects a fake estimator trained on outputs for the same prompt. The two roles share model parameters and, by default, optimizer states, while a separate frozen pretrained teacher provides the same reference guidance as in S2-Avatar.

Streaming video requires the estimator to track outputs generated with a causal history. We integrate condition shifting into S2-Avatar’s Self-Replay Forcing (SRF), which trains on replayed segments of the model’s own generated sequences (Zhang et al., 2026c). The shared fake estimator is fitted to these replay outputs, and its clean-latent predictions are compared with those of the frozen teacher to construct a detached correction for the generator. We retain S2’s replay procedure and perceptual regularization, as described in .

We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos through a 70-case human study and all 320 StreamAV-Bench scenarios. Relative to S2-Avatar, APEX receives positive net human preference for instruction following, consistency, and video quality, and achieves higher video instruction-fulfillment scores and visual aesthetics on both benchmark tracks. A separate measurement under matched training settings shows 4.4%4.4\% lower peak allocated GPU memory and 9.2%9.2\% shorter mean iteration time than DMD. Instruction-following preference also remains positive at 2 backbone NFE. also reports audiovisual synchronization, motion quality, and usability.

The paper makes three contributions to few-step streaming video generation:

  1. 1.

    Shared-network estimation through condition shifting. We learn the fake velocity within the generator while retaining a frozen reference teacher and removing the independent fake network.

  2. 2.

    Integration with Self-Replay Forcing. We apply condition-shifted estimation to the outputs of S2’s Self-Replay Forcing, retaining its replay procedure and perceptual regularization.

  3. 3.

    Video quality and training efficiency. We evaluate 180-second generation on 70 paired cases and all 320 StreamAV-Bench scenarios, alongside training-cost and sampling comparisons.

2 Preliminaries

We use 𝐱\mathbf{x} for a data latent, 𝐳\mathbf{z} for Gaussian noise, 𝐜\mathbf{c} for projected text, and 𝑭θ\bm{F}_{\theta} for a velocity predictor. The operator sg\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits denotes stop-gradient, and defines the video context.

Continuous Generative Models.

Conditional diffusion (Ho et al., 2020, Song et al., 2020) and flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022) transport Gaussian noise 𝐳∼pz=𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}\sim p_{z}=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) to data 𝐱∼pr(⋅∣𝐜)\mathbf{x}\sim p_{r}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{c}). For t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], we use the linear interpolation path of optimal transport (OT) flow matching:

𝐱t=t​𝐳+(1−t)​𝐱.\mathbf{x}_{t}=t\mathbf{z}+(1-t)\mathbf{x}\,. (1)

Sampling transports noise 𝐱1=𝐳\mathbf{x}_{1}=\mathbf{z} to data 𝐱0=𝐱\mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{x} along the probability-flow ODE:

d​𝐱td​t=𝐯⁡(𝐱t,t,𝐜).\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})\,. (2)

Flow matching learns this velocity field by regressing to the known target 𝐮r​(𝐱,𝐳):=𝐳−𝐱\mathbf{u}_{r}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}):=\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{x}:

ℒFM​(θ)=𝔼𝐱,𝐜,𝐳,t​[‖𝑭θ​(𝐱t,t,𝐜)−𝐮r​(𝐱,𝐳)‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)={\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{c},\,\mathbf{z},\,t}\left[\|\bm{F}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{u}_{r}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})\|^{2}\right]\,. (3)

The expectation uses paired data (𝐱,𝐜)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}), independent 𝐳∼pz\mathbf{z}\sim p_{z}, and t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1). The population minimizer is the conditional mean velocity 𝐯r∗(𝐱t,t,𝐜)=𝔼[𝐳−𝐱∣𝐱t,t,𝐜]\mathbf{v}_{r}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c}]. Sampling integrates from t=1t=1 to t=0t=0 with numerical ODE solvers (Karras et al., 2022), such as the first-order Euler method.

Few-Step Generation.

Consistency and interval-mapping methods support few-step sampling (Song et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2025b, Sun and Lin, 2025, Geng et al., 2025). The one-step Euler map is 𝑮θ​(𝐳,𝐜)=𝐳−𝑭θ​(𝐳,1,𝐜)\bm{G}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{z}-\bm{F}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},1,\mathbf{c}), with no destination-time input to the velocity predictor.

Distribution Matching.

For a fixed condition, let pθp_{\theta} be the distribution of 𝑮θ​(𝐳,𝐜)\bm{G}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c}) and prp_{r} the reference distribution. Their noised marginals at time tt have scores 𝐬i,t​(𝐲):=∇𝐲​log​pi,t​(𝐲)\mathbf{s}_{i,t}(\mathbf{y}):=\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\log p_{i,t}(\mathbf{y}) for i∈{r,θ}i\in\{r,\theta\}. DMD (Yin et al., 2024b) estimates the reverse-KL gradient using their score difference at the same noised generated sample. It uses a pretrained reference score and an auxiliary fake-score network trained on current outputs. expresses this score difference through marginal velocities under the OT path.

TwinFlow (Cheng et al., 2026) learns both velocities within one model, using positive time for the real trajectory and negative time for the fake trajectory. APEX selects the fake estimator through the condition input. Our video implementation shares the generator and fake estimator and retains S2’s frozen teacher for the reference prediction. relates the GAN gradient to a weighted score difference.

2.1 Autoregressive Video Generation and Self-Replay Forcing

We express S2-Avatar’s causal predictor and Self-Replay Forcing procedure (Zhang et al., 2026c) in APEX notation. For block ii, let 𝐱i\mathbf{x}^{i} denote the video latent and 𝐜i\mathbf{c}^{i} its text representation. The context 𝐡i\mathbf{h}^{i} contains the reference image, the preceding video states, and any accompanying audio. The diffusion time ti∈(0,1]t_{i}\in(0,1] is its noise level, with larger values indicating more noise. The clean prediction is

𝐱^0i=𝐱tii−ti​𝑭θ​(𝐱tii,ti,𝐜i∣𝐡i).\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}=\mathbf{x}_{t_{i}}^{i}-t_{i}\bm{F}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t_{i}}^{i},t_{i},\mathbf{c}^{i}\mid\mathbf{h}^{i}). (4)

A block-wise causal mask lets each block attend to its own tokens, conditions, and preceding video blocks.

Self-Replay Forcing.

Following S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c), we generate a detached autoregressive rollout (Huang et al., 2026a) and re-noise a sampled segment with diffusion forcing (DF) (Chen et al., 2024). One differentiable causal pass processes this segment, with each block reading preceding blocks at their replay noise levels. This allows cross-block gradients within the segment while keeping the external history and original rollout detached. We retain S2’s teacher and perceptual regularization (Zhang et al., 2026d) and replace DMD’s fake estimator (Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a) through condition shifting in .

3 Condition Shifting for Streaming Video Generation

We apply APEX’s condition shifting (Liu et al., 2026c) to the fake estimator in S2’s Self-Replay Forcing framework. The generator and fake estimator share parameters θ\theta, with a frozen teacher 𝑭ϕ\bm{F}_{\phi} providing S2’s reference prediction and guidance. compares DMD and APEX during training.

3.1 Condition Shifting on Generated Video

The network generates under 𝐜i\mathbf{c}^{i} and estimates the fake velocity from these outputs under 𝐜shifti=−𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{shift}}^{i}=-\mathbf{c}^{i}. We negate projected text before the transformer blocks, with positive diffusion times in both calls.

The NN evaluated blocks 𝐱θ1:N\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N} include replay outputs and any detached prefix from . We detach them and re-noise at a scoring time t′∈(0,1)t^{\prime}\in(0,1) with fresh Gaussian noise ϵ′∼pz\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}\sim p_{z}:

𝐱θ1:N,sg:=sg(𝐱θ1:N),𝐱θ,t′1:N,sg:=(1−t′)𝐱θ1:N,sg+t′ϵ′.\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}:=\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits(\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N}),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{1:N,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}:=(1-t^{\prime})\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}+t^{\prime}\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}. (5)

We draw a single scoring time t′t^{\prime} for all generated blocks in a sequence, separately from the replay times tit_{i} used to produce the clean predictions. With reference-image and audio conditions fixed and omitted from the notation, the shifted-condition network predicts the fake velocity from the re-noised video latents:

𝐯^θ,t′1:N:=𝑭θ(𝐱θ,t′1:N,sg,t′,𝐜shift1:N).\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{1:N}:=\bm{F}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{1:N,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits},t^{\prime},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{shift}}^{1:N}). (6)

To learn the velocity field of the generated samples, we use the following flow-matching loss with causal attention over the current and preceding noisy blocks, without an additional clean-video stream:

ℒfake(θ)=𝔼[MSE(𝐯^θ,t′1:N,ϵ′−𝐱θ1:N,sg)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fake}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{MSE}\!\left(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{1:N},\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}\right)\right]. (7)

Here MSE is the mean squared error with S2’s video weighting and averaging. Detaching the generated sequence and regression target restricts this update to the shifted-condition prediction.

3.2 A Detached Correction from the Velocity Difference

We form the generator correction from the frozen teacher’s 𝐱^0,r1:N\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,r}^{1:N} and fake clean-latent predictions at the same noisy video and scoring time, retaining S2’s conditioning, guidance, and DMD target (Zhang et al., 2026c, Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a). Here rr marks the teacher prediction and θ\theta the fake estimate.

𝐱^0,θi=𝐱θ,t′i,sg−t′​𝐯^θ,t′i,𝐯^r,t′i:=𝐱θ,t′i,sg−𝐱^0,rit′.\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,\theta}^{i}=\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{i,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}-t^{\prime}\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{i},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{r,t^{\prime}}^{i}:=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{i,\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}-\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,r}^{i}}{t^{\prime}}. (8)

Their clean-latent difference is proportional to the velocity difference at the same scoring time:

𝐱^0,ri−𝐱^0,θi=t′​𝐝^t′i,𝐝^t′i:=𝐯^θ,t′i−𝐯^r,t′i.\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,r}^{i}-\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,\theta}^{i}=t^{\prime}\widehat{\mathbf{d}}_{t^{\prime}}^{i},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{d}}_{t^{\prime}}^{i}:=\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{i}-\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{r,t^{\prime}}^{i}. (9)

We normalize this clean-latent difference as in to obtain 𝐝~t′1:N\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{t^{\prime}}^{1:N} and add it to the current output, giving the generator a detached regression target for the replay predictions:

ℒscore(θ)=𝔼[MSE(𝐱θ1:N,sg(𝐱θ1:N+𝐝~t′1:N))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{score}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{MSE}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N},\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{1:N}+\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{t^{\prime}}^{1:N}\right)\right)\right]. (10)

We hold the target fixed, including estimator predictions and normalization. Gradients therefore pass through replay outputs and their connected causal representations within the active segment.

Under the OT path, velocity estimates induce score estimates satisfying

𝐝^t′i=−t′1−t′​(𝐬^θ,t′i−𝐬^r,t′i).\widehat{\mathbf{d}}_{t^{\prime}}^{i}=-\frac{t^{\prime}}{1-t^{\prime}}\left(\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{i}-\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{r,t^{\prime}}^{i}\right). (11)

Interpreting these induced estimates as true conditional scores requires calibrated fields under common conditioning. derives the gradient of and discusses its score interpretation.

3.3 Shared-Parameter Updates

Following S2, the generator objective combines distribution matching and perceptual regularization:

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒscore​(θ)+ℒperc​(θ).\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{score}}(\theta)+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{perc}}(\theta). (12)

Generator updates alternate with fake estimation in on shared parameters θ\theta, retaining S2’s perceptual regularization (Zhang et al., 2026c, Zhang et al., 2026d) and keeping ϕ\phi frozen. By default, these updates share AdamW states, with separate states evaluated in . At inference, the original projected text selects generation with the chosen few-step schedule, followed by the common one-step spatial Refiner.

4 Evaluation

We evaluate 180-second streaming generation on ten StreamAV-Bench metrics and five human-preference dimensions, complemented by absolute ratings, usability, and training-cost and sampling comparisons.

4.1 Setting

Training data and model.

We reuse S2-Avatar’s complete training data and preparation pipeline (Zhang et al., 2026c), including filtering and annotation, for livestreams, talking heads, film and television, solo dance, and 2D/3D animation, as summarized in . APEX uses its causal audiovisual backbone and Self-Replay Forcing, sharing parameters and, by default, AdamW states for generator and fake updates.

Inference.

Unless otherwise specified, both models use 3 backbone denoising function evaluations (NFE) per generated block, excluding KV-cache encoding and updates. The common one-step 2×2\times spatial Refiner is counted separately. StreamAV-Bench outputs have resolution 1344×7681344\times 768.

StreamAV-Bench.

Following the experimental setup of Vidu S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c), we use all 160 Progressive and 160 Interactive scenarios of StreamAV-Bench (Liu et al., 2026f). The metrics cover instruction fulfillment (VIF, AIF), visual quality and aesthetics (VQ, VA), audio quality (AQ, PQ), audiovisual alignment and synchronization (AVAlign, AVSync), and subject and background consistency (SC, BC). All metrics are higher-is-better except AVSync, which measures temporal offset error in seconds. The 12-model comparison uses Progressive cases for VIF, AIF, SC, and BC, and both tracks for the remaining metrics.

Human evaluation.

We invited experts with backgrounds in art or aesthetics to provide preference ratings for 70 pairs of image-to-video (I2V) sequences across five dimensions: consistency, instruction following, audiovisual synchronization, video quality, and motion quality. Good/Same/Bad (GSB) denote wins, ties, and losses relative to S2-Avatar at 3 NFE. Net preference is 100​(G−B)/70100(G-B)/70, retaining ties in the denominator. Usability requires Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) above 2 for both instruction following and synchronization.

4.2 Results

Qualitative comparison.

compares 3-NFE I2V outputs using the same reference images and timestamps. APEX retains both bags late in one sequence and moves the tube toward the other hand for the applying instruction in another, illustrating object persistence and a prompt-directed change in hand pose.

Benchmark results.

APEX ranks first on VA, VIF, and AIF and second on VQ among the 12 models with available results in . In , VIF, AIF, and VA improve on both tracks, with Progressive VIF and AIF increasing by 0.025 and 0.067. VQ rises on Progressive (+0.049+0.049) but falls on Interactive (−0.070-0.070), yielding −0.011-0.011 overall. BC shows the opposite track-level pattern. AQ, AVAlign, and SC decrease on both tracks, pooled PQ is effectively unchanged, and pooled AVSync error rises from 1.319 to 1.341 s. These results show instruction and aesthetic gains alongside visual and audiovisual trade-offs.

Human evaluation.

and show the strongest preference for instruction following: 22 wins, 47 ties, and 1 loss yield +30.0%+30.0\% net preference, with MOS of 4.17 versus 3.99. Consistency and video quality each receive +4.3%+4.3\%, corresponding to three net wins. Audiovisual synchronization is tied in 69 of 70 pairs, with one loss (−1.4%-1.4\%) and MOS of 4.23 versus 4.26. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar (−8.6%-8.6\%). Both models meet the usability criterion for 62 of 70 evaluated I2V sequences (88.6%88.6\%).

4.3 Training and Sampling Comparisons

Additional preference evaluations use separate rounds of 70 paired 180-second I2V sequences, each against S2-Avatar at 3 NFE with the same Refiner. groups results by comparison round.

Training cost.

In a separate measurement under matched training settings (), peak allocated memory decreases from 102.7 to 98.2 GiB per GPU, saving 4.5 GiB (4.4%4.4\%) relative to DMD. Mean iteration time decreases from 35.9 to 32.6 s, a reduction of 3.3 s (9.2%9.2\%), while retaining the frozen teacher.

Two-step generation.

Against S2-Avatar at 3 NFE, APEX at 2 NFE receives +27.1%+27.1\% instruction preference (22 wins, 45 ties, 3 losses), while S2-Avatar at 2 NFE receives +2.9%+2.9\% in a separate paired round, as shown in . APEX’s other margins are negative: −2.9%-2.9\% for consistency and video quality, and −7.1%-7.1\% for synchronization and motion quality. compares APEX at 2 NFE with S2-Avatar at 3 NFE, showing broadly similar character appearance with differences in pose and fine detail.

Timestep sampling.

We vary the sampling of replay times tit_{i} over (0.75,0.9375,0.99)(0.75,0.9375,0.99), leaving the scoring-time schedule for t′t^{\prime} unchanged. The default uses equal weights, whereas DF4 and DF10 use (4,1,1)(4,1,1) and (10,1,1)(10,1,1), raising the probability of drawing the lowest noise level from 1/31/3 to 2/32/3 and 5/65/6. Sampled times are sorted along the replay segment before the differentiable pass. Default sampling has the highest instruction preference at both budgets in , reaching +27.1%+27.1\% at 2 NFE and +21.4%+21.4\% at 3 NFE. Other dimensions vary across both inference budgets, with no consistent advantage from favoring lower-noise replay.

Optimizer configurations.

reports results for shared optimizer states at 3 NFE and separate generator/fake optimizer states at 2 NFE. Both configurations use AdamW with shared model parameters, achieving instruction-following net preferences of +21.4%+21.4\% and +14.3%+14.3\%, respectively.

5 Conclusion

APEX integrates condition-shifted fake estimation into S2’s Self-Replay Forcing, sharing generator and fake parameters while retaining the frozen teacher. It improves instruction fulfillment and visual aesthetics, with positive human preference for instruction following at both 3 and 2 backbone NFE. Matched measurements show lower peak allocated GPU memory and shorter mean iteration time. Motion quality and audiovisual synchronization remain trade-offs, while APEX and S2-Avatar achieve the same usability rate.

Appendix A Related Work

A.1 Consistency and Trajectory-Based Generation

Diffusion (Ho et al., 2020, Song et al., 2020, Karras et al., 2022) and flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022) generate samples by integrating a learned velocity field from noise to data. Embedded Representation Warmup (Liu et al., 2025a) improves training efficiency by aligning early model layers with a pretrained encoder before full generative training. Consistency and trajectory-based methods train the model to predict over a time interval, allowing generation with fewer network evaluations. Consistency Models (CMs) (Song et al., 2023, Lu and Song, 2024) learn to map points on the same trajectory to a common endpoint. Score-regularized continuous-time consistency (rCM) combines consistency training with score-based distribution matching for large-scale diffusion distillation (Zheng et al., 2025b). MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025) predicts the average velocity over an interval, while Transition Models (TiM) (Wang et al., 2025) learn the transition between its endpoints. DuMo (Sun et al., 2026b) jointly predicts local velocity and a flow map with two heads on a shared backbone. UCGM (Sun et al., 2025b) interpolates between generative training objectives.

A.2 Distribution Matching and Adversarial Training

Few-step generation also benefits from direct feedback on the generated distribution.

External correction signals can come from auxiliary score models, as in distribution matching (Yin et al., 2024b, Yin et al., 2024a), or from discriminators used in adversarial refiners (Kim et al., 2023, Sauer et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2025a). Additional networks increase memory use and update cost. Some early distillation methods also use precomputed teacher-student pairs for regularization, while DMD2 removes that paired-data requirement (Yin et al., 2024a). Direct Discriminative Optimization (DDO) (Zheng et al., 2025a) expresses the GAN discriminator as a likelihood ratio constructed from the target and a fixed reference model.

TwinFlow (Cheng et al., 2026) learns real and fake trajectories within a shared model and uses their velocity discrepancy to construct an internal correction signal. LLaDA-Image Turbo (Chen et al., 2026a) adapts TwinFlow-based distillation to support image generation in two to four sampling steps.

APEX (Liu et al., 2026c) follows this line and separates the branches through condition shifting. The shifted condition selects the fake estimator for samples generated with the original prompt. In , our video formulation shares generator and fake parameters while retaining S2’s frozen reference teacher.

Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM) (Liu et al., 2026a) adds feature mean and standard deviation matching to DMD using the generator’s exponential moving average (EMA) copy.

Few-step score identity distillation (SiD) (Zhou et al., 2025) also studies how conditioning affects distribution matching. Its Zero-CFG strategy removes text conditioning from the fake-score network, while Anti-CFG applies negative classifier-free guidance by combining conditional and unconditional predictions. These strategies modify the fake-score estimate. APEX fits the fake velocity under shifted text.

Fake-Score-network-Free DMD (FSF-DMD) (Kim et al., 2026a) replaces the auxiliary fake-score network with a generator-induced endpoint pseudo-velocity. APEX instead learns the fake velocity through flow matching on generated samples under a shifted condition. TBSM (Sun et al., 2026a) constructs regression targets from attraction to real samples and repulsion from generated samples under an energy-distance objective; its correction is defined by sample interactions rather than a real/fake velocity difference.

A.3 Causal Streaming Video

Autoregressive video diffusion has been studied through asynchronous generation (Sun et al., 2025a), progressive prediction (Xie et al., 2025), and causal generation with cache sharing (Gao et al., 2025a). MAGI-1 studies autoregressive generation at scale (Teng et al., 2025), while SkyReels-V2 targets extended video generation (Chen et al., 2025). FIFO-Diffusion (Kim et al., 2024) and StreamingT2V (Henschel et al., 2025) also investigate extending video generation beyond a short clip. Later predictions depend on generated history.

CausVid distills bidirectional video diffusion into an autoregressive model (Yin et al., 2025); diagonal distillation provides another streaming autoregressive formulation (Liu et al., 2026d). Causal Forcing and Causal Forcing++ study few-step autoregressive distillation for real-time interaction (Zhu et al., 2026a, Zhao et al., 2026b). Causal-rCM unifies Teacher Forcing and Self Forcing in a streaming distillation recipe (Zheng et al., 2026). LPM studies video-based character performance (Zeng et al., 2026), providing a setting for distribution matching in autoregressive models that animate characters.

S2-Avatar (Zhang et al., 2026c) combines bidirectional reference-conditioned training, causal adaptation with Teacher and Diffusion Forcing, and Self-Replay Forcing. Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024) exposes the model to noisy historical states, while Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2026a) trains with autoregressive histories generated by the current model. S2’s replay procedure retains cross-block gradients inside a sampled trajectory segment without retaining the full rollout graph. APEX uses this video setting to learn the fake estimator within the generator while retaining S2’s causal replay procedure and reference teacher. FlowCPO (Han et al., 2026) studies offline preference alignment using fixed preferred and dispreferred samples. Preference optimization and latent refinement are separate from the APEX correction.

A.4 Historical Context and Long Video Generation

History-Guided Video Diffusion studies conditioning on past video (Song et al., 2025), while Grounded Forcing separates persistent semantics from recent dynamics (Chen et al., 2026b). LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a) and Rolling Forcing (Liu et al., 2025b) target real-time long video generation; Infinity-RoPE investigates action control under autoregressive self-rollout (Yesiltepe et al., 2026). UltraViCo (Zhao et al., 2026a) addresses length extrapolation by suppressing attention dispersion beyond the training window, providing a complementary approach to extending video duration. These works motivate evaluating instruction response and motion quality alongside visual appearance as a stream grows longer.

Memory design provides a complementary approach. SWIFT uses prompt-adaptive memory (Tan et al., 2026), IAMFlow studies identity-aware memory (Liu et al., 2026e), and FramePack compresses the input-frame context for next-frame prediction (Zhang and Agrawala, 2025). Deep Forcing uses sink states and compression (Yi et al., 2025); Rolling Sink studies the gap between limited training horizons and open-ended testing (Li et al., 2026b). MemRoPE uses evolving memory tokens for extended generation (Kim et al., 2026b). Attention sinks were also studied for streaming language models (Xiao et al., 2024); S2 adopts sink blocks within its video context design (Zhang et al., 2026d, Zhang et al., 2026c). APEX retains this context design for its shared model. Quant VideoGen (Xi et al., 2026) reduces autoregressive history-storage costs through two-bit KV-cache quantization, using semantic-aware smoothing and progressive residual quantization. ViewRope (Xiang et al., 2026) instead injects camera-ray geometry into rotary position embeddings and selects relevant historical frames to improve spatial consistency in camera-controlled video world models. These methods address history storage and retrieval, complementing APEX’s focus on the training cost of distribution estimation.

For streaming video understanding, ChronoReplay (Hu et al., 2026a) organizes heterogeneous spatial supervision into chronological episodes, while Supervising the Visible State (Hu et al., 2026b) separates supervision of temporal state from adaptive selection of visual evidence. These studies provide complementary context for the role of temporal supervision and historical evidence in streaming video understanding.

A.5 Audio-Driven and Interactive Video

Audio-driven character generation includes portrait animation with Hallo3 (Cui et al., 2025), body animation with OmniAvatar (Gan et al., 2025), and cinematic video with Wan-S2V (Gao et al., 2025b). StableAvatar studies extended audio-driven generation (Tu et al., 2025). Live Avatar (Huang et al., 2025), SoulX-FlashTalk (Shen et al., 2025), and AptAvatar (Zhang et al., 2026a) address real-time or long-form avatar generation. AvatarForcing specifically studies one-step streaming talking avatars (Cui et al., 2026). Joint audio and video generation is studied by OmniForcing (Su et al., 2026b), Hallo-Live (Li et al., 2026a), and Omni-LiveAvatar (Zhu et al., 2026b). TurboT2VA (Yang et al., 2026) extends consistency distillation to joint video-audio generation with modality-specific normalization and a progressive curriculum that introduces distribution matching after consistency training. This connects few-step distillation to audiovisual synchronization, although its joint-generation setting differs from the causal replay setting studied here. Comparisons must distinguish joint audio generation from video generation conditioned on fixed external audio.

S2’s evaluation also includes external systems such as PixVerse R1 (PixVerse, 2026), HappyOyster (Alibaba, 2026), Odyssey-2 (Odyssey, 2025), and HeyGen (HeyGen, 2026). Their inclusion in S2 provides evaluation context; the APEX evidence here consists of the internal I2V comparison and the completed StreamAV-Bench run in . Comparisons must match references, audio, duration, and resolution.

A.6 Efficient Video Inference

Sampling steps are one component of generation cost. TurboDiffusion accelerates video diffusion (Zhang et al., 2025h), and TurboServe addresses efficient streaming service (Jiang et al., 2026). Pyramidal Flow Matching studies efficient video generation across scales (Jin et al., 2025); the present experiments account separately for the low-resolution backbone and one-step high-resolution spatial Refiner.

Efficient attention methods can be organized into hardware-efficient, sparse, compact, and linear approaches (Zhang et al., 2025b). Sparse VideoGen (Xi et al., 2025) exploits spatial and temporal attention-head patterns, while Sparse VideoGen2 (Yang et al., 2025b) uses semantic-aware token permutation to identify and group important attention blocks. SVG-EAR (Zhou et al., 2026) complements sparse computation with parameter-free centroid compensation and error-aware routing for skipped blocks.

S2’s attention implementation draws on several families of efficient operators. SageAttention and SageAttention2 use low-bit attention (Zhang et al., 2025e, Zhang et al., 2025a); SageAttention2++ improves its implementation (Zhang et al., 2025g), and SageAttention3 explores FP4 inference and low-bit training (Zhang et al., 2025d). SageBwd further studies trainable low-bit attention (Zhang et al., 2026b). SpargeAttention studies sparse attention without additional training (Zhang et al., 2025f), while SpargeAttention2 uses trainable masking and distillation (Zhang et al., 2026e). SLA and SLA2 combine sparse and linear attention. SLA2 incorporates learnable routing together with quantization-aware training (Zhang et al., 2025c, Zhang et al., 2026f).

At the linear-layer level, 6Bit-Diffusion (Su et al., 2026a) dynamically allocates NVFP4 and INT8 precision according to quantization sensitivity and reuses temporally stable block residuals. Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Video Generation (Hu and Zhang, 2026) uses a smaller model to draft video blocks and a quality router to decide which blocks require regeneration by the larger target model. Both affect inference computation, a separate consideration from the number of networks maintained during distillation.

S2 also draws on block-level low-bit computation (Zhang et al., 2025i) and Ulysses-style parallelism (Jacobs et al., 2023). These operators, precision choices, and parallel schedules can change latency at the same NFE. The training-cost comparison in measures APEX and DMD under matched settings.

A.7 Streaming Video Editing

StreamDiffusionV2 studies dynamic interactive video generation (Feng et al., 2025). LiveEdit (Wang et al., 2026), JoyAI-Video-Edit (Xiao et al., 2026), and SANA-Streaming (Zhao et al., 2026c) address streaming video editing. These methods use an incoming video’s motion and structure, which differs from I2V conditioning.

Interactive streaming evaluation.

StreamEval (StreamEval Team, 2026) evaluates timed interactions across avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, measuring task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. Our reported benchmark results use StreamAV-Bench (Liu et al., 2026f) and do not include StreamEval measurements.

Visual text evaluation.

VTR-Bench (Huang et al., 2026b) evaluates visual text fidelity separately from scene and motion requirements in video. UltraText Bench (Liu et al., 2026b) evaluates dense bilingual text in individual images, providing complementary background on visual text rendering. Neither is evaluated here.

Appendix B Theoretical Analysis and Proofs

We derive the OT score-velocity identity and the frozen-target gradient in . The endpoint formulation in compares clean-latent and velocity losses algebraically. The score identities fix conditioning; the replay gradient differentiates connected predictions with the target fixed. These results do not establish long-horizon stability or an exact KL gradient for the joint video trajectory.

B.1 Setup

We use bold lowercase letters for vectors like 𝐱,𝐳,𝐯\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},\mathbf{v} and bold uppercase letters for matrices and operators like 𝑭\bm{F}. The identity matrix is denoted by 𝐈\mathbf{I}, and 𝟎\mathbf{0} represents the zero vector.

Additional video conditions 𝐡\mathbf{h} are held fixed and suppressed, as is 𝐜\mathbf{c} when unambiguous. Throughout this appendix, we work with the Optimal Transport (OT) interpolation path defined by:

𝐱t=t​𝐳+(1−t)​𝐱,t∈[0,1],\mathbf{x}_{t}=t\mathbf{z}+(1-t)\mathbf{x},\quad t\in[0,1], (13)

𝐮r​(𝐱,𝐳):=𝐳−𝐱.\mathbf{u}_{r}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}):=\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{x}. (14)

The population real-data velocity is the conditional mean of this target:

𝐯r∗(𝐱t,t):=𝔼[𝐮r(𝐱,𝐳)∣𝐱t,t].\mathbf{v}_{r}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t):=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{u}_{r}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]. (15)

A star marks a population conditional mean, distinct from a network estimate.

We write 𝑭θ\bm{F}_{\theta} for the velocity estimate 𝑭θ​(𝐱t,t,𝐜)∈ℝd\bm{F}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} when its inputs are clear.

For θ∈ℝP\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{P} and a vector output 𝐪∈ℝd\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, Jθ​𝐪:=∂𝐪/∂θ∈ℝd×PJ_{\theta}\mathbf{q}:=\partial\mathbf{q}/\partial\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P}, so the chain rule uses its transpose to map output derivatives to parameter gradients.

The one-step map 𝑮θ​(𝐳,𝐜)=𝐳−𝑭θ​(𝐳,1,𝐜)\bm{G}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{z}-\bm{F}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},1,\mathbf{c}) and S2’s clean-latent conversion use this same parameterization.

B.2 Score-Velocity Duality under OT Path

The OT path gives a score-velocity identity for both real and generated endpoint distributions.

Proposition B.1 (Score-Velocity Duality) .

Let 𝐱t=t​𝐳+(1−t)​𝐱\mathbf{x}_{t}=t\mathbf{z}+(1-t)\mathbf{x} for t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), with independent draws 𝐳∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and 𝐱∼pr\mathbf{x}\sim p_{r}. Write pr,tp_{r,t} for the density of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. The optimal least-squares velocity is

𝐯r∗(𝐱t,t):=𝔼[𝐮r(𝐱,𝐳)∣𝐱t,t].\mathbf{v}_{r}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t):=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{u}_{r}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t]. (17)

Then the score function 𝐬r,t​(𝐱t):=∇𝐱t​log​pr,t​(𝐱t)\mathbf{s}_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}):=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) along the OT path satisfies

𝐬r,t​(𝐱t)=−𝐱t+(1−t)​𝐯r∗​(𝐱t,t)t.\mathbf{s}_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=-\frac{\mathbf{x}_{t}+(1-t)\mathbf{v}_{r}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)}{t}. (18)

𝔼⁡[𝐱′∣𝐱t]=𝐱t+t2​∇𝐱t​log⁡pr,t​(𝐱t)=𝐱t+t2​𝐬r,t​(𝐱t).\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}]=\mathbf{x}_{t}+t^{2}\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\mathbf{x}_{t}+t^{2}\,\mathbf{s}_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}). (19)

Since 𝐱′=(1−t)​𝐱\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}, we recover the conditional expectation of the original clean endpoint 𝐱\mathbf{x}:

=11−t​[𝐱t+t2​𝐬r,t​(𝐱t)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-t}\left[\mathbf{x}_{t}+t^{2}\,\mathbf{s}_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right]
=𝐱t+t2​𝐬r,t​(𝐱t)1−t.\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{t}+t^{2}\,\mathbf{s}_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}{1-t}. (20)

𝐳=𝐱t−(1−t)​𝐱t.\mathbf{z}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{t}-(1-t)\mathbf{x}}{t}.

Suppressing block indices, let 𝐱^0,r\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,r} be the guided prediction of the frozen teacher and 𝐱^0,θ=𝐱θ,t′sg−t′​𝐯^θ,t′\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,\theta}=\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}^{\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits}-t^{\prime}\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t^{\prime}} the fake clean-latent prediction. The mean uses the inherited video mask and is computed per video across the full scored sequence, including any detached rollout prefix. It is not recomputed separately for each block. Both estimator predictions and the normalization ww stay fixed when differentiating the generator loss with respect to θ\theta.

For the derivative, write 𝐱θ\mathbf{x}_{\theta} and 𝐝~t′\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}_{t^{\prime}} as the masked vectors of dd coordinates used by the MSE, and let J:=∂𝐱θ/∂θJ:=\partial\mathbf{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta. Rows of JJ for the detached prefix are zero, while replay outputs retain derivatives through the connected causal representations inside the active segment. This is the exact gradient of the stated frozen-target surrogate. For a one-step map 𝑮θ=𝐳−𝑭θ\bm{G}_{\theta}=\mathbf{z}-\bm{F}_{\theta}, the endpoint target 𝐱θ+𝐝~\mathbf{x}_{\theta}+\widetilde{\mathbf{d}} corresponds to the velocity target 𝑭θ−𝐝~\bm{F}_{\theta}-\widetilde{\mathbf{d}}. B.5 Endpoint-Velocity Equivalence

We prove that the endpoint-space MSE and velocity-space MSE are equivalent up to a scalar factor t2t^{2}. Comparing weighted losses therefore requires accounting for this time-dependent factor.

‖𝒇𝐱​(𝑭θ,𝐱t,t)−𝒇𝐱​(𝐯^θ,t,𝐱t,t)‖22\displaystyle\bigl\|\bm{f}^{\mathbf{x}}(\bm{F}_{\theta},\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\bm{f}^{\mathbf{x}}(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t},\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\bigr\|_{2}^{2} =‖t⁡(𝐯^θ,t−𝑭θ)‖22\displaystyle=\bigl\|t\,(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t}-\bm{F}_{\theta})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}

which proves for both endpoint predictions at the same state and time.

B.6 Gradient Equivalence of Alternative Loss

We now show that the gradient of the mixed endpoint loss ℒmix\mathcal{L}_{\text{mix}} is equal to the gradient of the alternative loss 𝒢APEX \mathcal{G}_{\text{{APEX} }}. This equivalence holds when the mixed target is detached during differentiation.

Consider ℒmix\mathcal{L}_{\text{mix}} from and 𝒢APEX \mathcal{G}_{\text{{APEX} }} from .

∇θℒmix​(θ)=∇θ𝒢APEX ​(θ).\nabla_{\theta}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{mix}}(\theta)=\nabla_{\theta}\,\mathcal{G}_{\text{{APEX} }}(\theta). (49)

All expectations below use real-data pairs (𝐱,𝐜)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}), independent noise 𝐳∼pz\mathbf{z}\sim p_{z}, and the sampled time t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1); 𝐱t=(1−t)​𝐱+t​𝐳\mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{z}. Proposition B.11 (Score-Difference Form) .

Let 𝐯^r,t\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{r,t} and 𝐯^θ,t\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta,t} be the original- and shifted-condition predictions from , evaluated at (𝐱t,𝐜)(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{c}). ∇θ𝒢APEX=−2​𝔼​[t2​Jt⊤​sg(𝐬^r,t−𝐬^mix,t)].\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{APEX}}=-2\mathbb{E}\!\left[t^{2}J_{t}^{\top}\mathop{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\operatorname{sg}}}\nolimits\!\left(\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{r,t}-\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{\mathrm{mix},t}\right)\right]. (72)

Remark B.13 (Scope of the gradient identity) .

This identity rewrites the frozen-target gradient of the endpoint objective. It does not require the network-induced fields 𝐬^r,t\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{r,t} and 𝐬^θ,t\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta,t} to equal true distribution scores, and it does not identify the loss with a divergence between generated and data distributions. The coefficient is constant across samples only at a fixed time; the residual and network Jacobian still vary across samples.

Remark B.14 (When the mixed field has a density interpretation) .

For each fixed tt, pθ,tendp_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{end}} is the law of (1−t)​𝐱θend​(t)+t​ϵ′(1-t)\mathbf{x}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{end}}(t)+t\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime} from , with independent Gaussian ϵ′\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime}. The clean endpoint law itself depends on tt; the score conversion applies at each fixed time. If the shifted-condition field is calibrated so that 𝐬^θ,t=∇log⁡pθ,tend\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{\theta,t}=\nabla\log p_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{end}}, then 𝐬^mix,t\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{\mathrm{mix},t} is the score of the following geometric combination:

pmix,t​(𝐱t∣𝐜)∝pr,t​(𝐱t∣𝐜)1−λ​[pθ,tend​(𝐱t∣𝐜)]λ,p_{\mathrm{mix},t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{c})\propto p_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{c})^{1-\lambda}\left[p_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{end}}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{c})\right]^{\lambda}, (78)

provided this expression is normalizable. This is a geometric combination at a fixed time, and need not define a consistent probability path across time. Without calibration, 𝐬^mix,t\widehat{\mathbf{s}}_{\mathrm{mix},t} need not be a density score.

Relation to GAN weighting.

For comparison, define the noised generated sample 𝐱θ,t:=(1−t)​𝑮θ​(𝐳,𝐜)+t​ϵ′\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t}:=(1-t)\bm{G}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c})+t\bm{\epsilon}^{\prime} and its Jacobian JtG:=Jθ​𝐱θ,tJ_{t}^{G}:=J_{\theta}\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t}. At fixed noise, the non-saturating GAN gradient takes the form

∇θℒNS​-​GAN=𝔼⁡[(JtG)⊤​wNS​(𝐱θ,t)​(𝐬θ,t​(𝐱θ,t)−𝐬r,t​(𝐱θ,t))],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NS\text{-}GAN}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(J_{t}^{G})^{\top}\,w_{\mathrm{NS}}(\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t})\left(\mathbf{s}_{\theta,t}(\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t})-\mathbf{s}_{r,t}(\mathbf{x}_{\theta,t})\right)\right], (79)

where wNS=1−Dt∗w_{\mathrm{NS}}=1-D_{t}^{*} for the optimal discriminator held fixed during the generator update. Unlike this discriminator-dependent weight, the explicit coefficient in depends only on time. Each gradient uses its own expectation and Jacobian; this comparison concerns sample weighting.

B.8 GAN Dynamics and Score-Difference Gradients

Let pθ​(𝐱)p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) and pr​(𝐱)p_{r}(\mathbf{x}) denote the generated and data densities for a fixed condition 𝐜\mathbf{c}, omitted below for brevity, and let 𝐬⁡(𝐱):=∇𝐱​log​p​(𝐱)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}):=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p(\mathbf{x}) denote a distribution’s score. With the optimal discriminator D∗​(𝐱)=pr​(𝐱)/pr​(𝐱)+pθ​(𝐱)D^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\nicefrac{{p_{r}(\mathbf{x})}}{{p_{r}(\mathbf{x})+p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}} held fixed during the generator update (Mohamed and Lakshminarayanan, 2016, Goodfellow et al., 2014), the saturating and non-saturating losses yield a weighted score-difference gradient:

∇θℒGAN∝𝔼𝐱∼pθ​[(∂𝐱∂θ)⊤​wGAN​(𝐱)​(𝐬θ​(𝐱)−𝐬r​(𝐱))].\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}\propto{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{\theta}}\left[\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\top}w_{\mathrm{GAN}}(\mathbf{x})\bigl(\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{s}_{r}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\right]\,. (80)

For 𝐱=𝑮θ​(𝐳,𝐜)\mathbf{x}=\bm{G}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c}), the weights are wGAN​(𝐱)=D∗​(𝐱)w_{\mathrm{GAN}}(\mathbf{x})=D^{*}(\mathbf{x}) (saturating) and wGAN​(𝐱)=1−D∗​(𝐱)w_{\mathrm{GAN}}(\mathbf{x})=1-D^{*}(\mathbf{x}) (non-saturating).

Appendix C Training Data

We reuse the complete S2-Avatar training data and preparation pipeline, including filtering and annotation (Zhang et al., 2026c). The data include livestream and talking-head videos, film and television, solo dance, and 2D/3D animation, covering facial expressions, body motion, and animated characters. summarizes the data pipeline inherited from Vidu S1 (Zhang et al., 2026d).

Single-shot clips are filtered for subject visibility, visual quality, content safety, shot stability, and interactivity. Smooth camera motion is corrected using background features after masking foreground subjects; clips with large or complex camera motion are excluded. Full-clip and event-aligned chunk captions describe actions and outcomes chronologically, using object detection and speech recognition to ground the annotations. The clipping, quality checks, background stabilization, and annotation procedures follow S2 without changes; APEX modifies only the model training procedure, as described in .

Appendix D Evaluation Details

We detail the evaluators, aggregation rules, and comparison budgets for and .

D.1 StreamAV-Bench

We evaluate all 320 StreamAV-Bench cases (Liu et al., 2026f): 160 Progressive and 160 Interactive scenarios, using 180-second outputs. The Interactive track introduces five runtime condition updates at 30-second intervals, at 30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 seconds. We measure APEX and S2-Avatar. Other models’ VIF scores are from StreamAV-Bench (Liu et al., 2026f), with other scores from Vidu S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c).

Visual Aesthetics (VA) uses the LAION Aesthetic Predictor (LAION-AI, 2022). Visual Quality (VQ), Video Instruction Fulfillment (VIF), Audio Quality (AQ), and Audio Instruction Fulfillment (AIF) use the benchmark’s Gemini judge. Subject Consistency (SC) and Background Consistency (BC) measure full-sequence stability. Audio-Visual Alignment (AVAlign) uses ImageBind similarity (Girdhar et al., 2023) to assess cross-modal semantic agreement. Audio-Visual Synchronization (AVSync) uses Synchformer (Iashin et al., 2024) to measure temporal offset error in seconds. Production Quality (PQ) assesses the output audio with AudioBox Aesthetics (Tjandra et al., 2025). All benchmark metrics except AVSync are higher-is-better.

VA, PQ, AVAlign, and AVSync are evaluated over six non-overlapping 30-second windows per video, whereas SC and BC use the full 180-second sequence. Track summaries average case-level scores with equal weight. Overall summaries pool all 320 cases. Since the tracks have equal size, this equals the average of the two unrounded track means. The 12-model comparison in uses Progressive cases for VIF, AIF, SC, and BC, and both tracks for the remaining metrics. provides track means and pooled results. Differences use unrounded APEX minus S2-Avatar scores, so a positive AVSync difference indicates worse synchronization.

D.2 Paired Human Comparisons

Each comparison uses 70 paired 180-second I2V cases. The five preference dimensions are consistency, instruction following, audiovisual synchronization, video quality, and motion quality. Good/Same/Bad (GSB) counts wins, ties, and losses for the evaluated model relative to the reference, with G+S+B=70G+S+B=70 for each dimension. Net preference is 100​(G−B)/70100(G-B)/70, retaining tied cases in the denominator. One net win therefore changes the reported preference by approximately 1.43 percentage points. Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) assess instruction following and synchronization, with higher values indicating better quality. A sequence is counted as usable when both scores exceed 2. Synchronization MOS and the benchmark’s AVSync error therefore have opposite directions. In the main study, consistency and video quality each have G/S/B counts of 13/47/10 (three net wins), whereas motion quality has 2/60/8 (six net losses), matching .

The main 3-NFE human study in and the additional sampling and training comparisons use separate evaluation rounds. groups the latter by sampling budget and optimizer configuration. Each additional variant is paired with S2-Avatar at 3 NFE, so differences between variants are comparisons against a common reference rather than direct pairwise judgments. For the optimizer comparisons, shared AdamW states are evaluated at 3 NFE and separate states at 2 NFE, with model parameters shared in both settings. All replay-time sampling variants share optimizer states and sort sampled times along the sequence. At noise levels (0.75,0.9375,0.99)(0.75,0.9375,0.99), the default, DF4, and DF10 weights correspond to sampling probabilities (1/3,1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3,1/3), (2/3,1/6,1/6)(2/3,1/6,1/6), and (5/6,1/12,1/12)(5/6,1/12,1/12), respectively. DF10 favors the lowest noise level most strongly.

D.3 Backbone and Refiner Budget

NFE counts backbone denoising evaluations per generated video block, excluding KV-cache encoding and updates. All paired comparisons use the same one-step spatial Refiner with 2×2\times upsampling, following S2 (Zhang et al., 2026c). The Refiner adds one separate evaluation per block to either a 2-NFE or a 3-NFE backbone. The 2-NFE setting therefore uses one third fewer backbone evaluations, with the Refiner unchanged. The teacher and fake estimator add no inference calls. The replay times tit_{i} and scoring time t′t^{\prime} in are variables used during training and do not determine the inference evaluation budget.
